content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.8. I used 44 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on three tasks that share no rules: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested new tasks chosen so that the number of new rules didn't line up with how much each task resembled the trained ones.

| Test tasks | New rules | Samples | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M3, L1-S1-M2, L3-S1-M2 | 0 | 15 | ~21 |
| L1-S1-M4, L4-S2-M3, L2-S4-M1 | 1 | 12 | ~37 |
| L4-S4-M1 | 2 | 4 | ~37 |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 10 | ~37 |

**Evidence for part-based:**
- **Overlap didn't predict cost.** L1-S1-M4 gives the same response as L1-S1-M1 on 75% of inputs and shares two of its rules. That's the most overlap of any task I tested, but it was among the slowest to learn.
- **Recombinations were cheap.** L1-S2-M3 shares only one rule with each trained task and has less overlap than L1-S1-M4, yet it was learned faster.
- **The pattern held across tasks.** Three different 0-new tasks were all cheap, and three different 1-new tasks were all costly, whichever dimension the new rule was on.

**Why not higher confidence:**
- **No rise from 1 to 3 new rules.** All three groups averaged about 37. A strict part-based learner should probably get more costly with each new rule; this looks more like a step between "no new rules" and "some new rules".
- **The noise is large.** Single results ranged from 1 to 77.
- **One alternative remains open.** I can't rule out a holistic learner whose hidden similarity measure happens to follow the rules.

I didn't spend the remaining 16 budget units. With this much noise, a 1-new versus 3-new difference of a few examples would have needed far more samples than were left.
